summary: This mishnah teaches which lulavim are not kosher: stolen, dried out, used for avodah zarah, or with a broken top or broken leaves. A lulav must be at least three tefachim long.

chunks.en: A lulav that is stolen or dried out
chunks.st: A lulav that was stolen or that is completely dry

chunks.he: פָּסוּל. שֶׁל אֲשֵׁרָה וְשֶׁל עִיר הַנִּדַּחַת,
chunks.en: is not kosher. One from an asheirah tree or from a city that served idols
chunks.st: is unfit for use in fulfilling the mitzva of the four species. The lulav of a tree worshipped as idolatry [asheira] and a lulav from a city whose residents were incited to idolatry,
chunks.stMore: which must be burned along with all the city’s property,

words.note: A tree that people worshipped as an idol.
A Jewish city where the people were led to serve idols.

chunks.en: is not kosher. If its top was cut off,
chunks.st: are unfit. If the top of the lulav was severed

chunks.en: or its leaves were broken off,
chunks.st: or if the palm leaves were severed from the spine of the lulav,

chunks.en: it is not kosher. If its leaves spread apart,
chunks.st: it is unfit. If its leaves, although still attached, were spread
chunks.stMore: and are no longer completely joined to the spine,

chunks.en: it is kosher. Rabbi Yehuda says,
chunks.st: it is fit. Rabbi Yehuda says:

chunks.en: he should tie it together at the top.
chunks.st: In that case, one should bind the lulav from the top,
chunks.stMore: to join the leaves that spread to the spine.

chunks.en: Lulavim from the palms of the Iron Mountain are kosher.
chunks.explain: Their leaves are short and do not cover the whole spine.
chunks.st: A lulav from the palms of the Iron Mountain are fit
chunks.stMore: for use, although it differs from one taken from a standard palm tree, in that its leaves are shorter and do not cover the entire spine.

chunks.en: A lulav that is three tefachim long,
chunks.st: A lulav that has three handbreadths

chunks.en: enough to shake it, is kosher.
chunks.st: in length, sufficient to enable one to wave with it, is fit for use in fulfilling the mitzva.

summary: A hadas (myrtle branch) that is stolen, dried out, used for avodah zarah, or broken is not kosher. If it has more berries than leaves, it can be fixed by picking off berries, but not on Yom Tov.

chunks.en: A hadas that is stolen or dried out
chunks.st: A myrtle branch that was stolen or that is completely dry

words.note: A myrtle branch, one of the four minim.

chunks.he: פָּסוּל. שֶׁל אֲשֵׁרָה וְשֶׁל עִיר הַנִּדַּחַת,
chunks.en: is not kosher. One from an asheirah tree or from a city that served idols
chunks.st: is unfit. A myrtle branch of a tree worshipped as idolatry [asheira] or a myrtle branch from a city whose residents were incited to idolatry

chunks.en: is not kosher. If its top was cut off,
chunks.st: is unfit. If the top of the myrtle branch was severed,

chunks.en: or its leaves were broken off, or
chunks.st: if the leaves were severed completely, or if

chunks.en: its berries were more than its leaves,
chunks.st: its berries were more numerous than its leaves,

chunks.en: it is not kosher. But if he made them fewer,
chunks.st: it is unfit. If one diminished their number by plucking berries so that they no longer outnumbered the leaves,

chunks.en: it is kosher. But we may not make them fewer on Yom Tov.
chunks.st: the myrtle branch is fit. But one may not diminish the number on the Festival itself.

summary: An aravah (willow branch) that is stolen, dried out, used for avodah zarah, or broken is not kosher. A tzaftzafa is not a real aravah. A wilted aravah, or one from a dry field, is kosher.

chunks.en: An aravah that is stolen or dried out
chunks.st: A willow branch that was stolen or is completely dry

words.note: A willow branch, one of the four minim.

chunks.he: פְּסוּלָה. שֶׁל אֲשֵׁרָה וְשֶׁל עִיר הַנִּדַּחַת,
chunks.en: is not kosher. One from an asheirah tree or from a city that served idols
chunks.st: is unfit. One from a tree worshipped as idolatry [asheira] or from a city whose residents were incited to idolatry

chunks.en: is not kosher. If its top was cut off,
chunks.st: is unfit. If the top was severed,

chunks.en: or its leaves were broken off,
chunks.st: or its leaves were severed,

chunks.en: or a tzaftzafa, it is not kosher.
chunks.explain: A tzaftzafa looks like a willow, but is a different kind of tree.
chunks.st: or if it is the tzaftzafa, a species similar to, but not actually a willow, it is unfit.

chunks.en: One that is wilted, or that lost a few of its leaves,
chunks.st: However, a willow branch that is slightly dried, and one that a minority of its leaves fell,

chunks.en: or that grew in a field without a river, is kosher.
chunks.st: and a branch from a willow that does not grow by the river, but instead is from a non-irrigated field, is fit.

summary: Rabbi Yishmael says we take three hadasim, two aravos, one lulav and one esrog. Rabbi Tarfon and Rabbi Akiva disagree about how many we need and if they may be cut at the top.

chunks.en: Rabbi Yishmael says,
chunks.st: Rabbi Yishmael says:

chunks.en: three hadasim and two aravos,
chunks.st: The mitzva of the four species is to take three myrtle branches, and two willow branches,

chunks.en: one lulav and one esrog,
chunks.st: one lulav, and one etrog.

chunks.he: אֲפִלּוּ שְׁנַיִם קְטוּמִים וְאֶחָד אֵינוֹ קָטוּם.
chunks.en: even if two hadasim are cut at the top and one is not cut.
chunks.st: With regard to the myrtle branches, even if the tops of two are severed and the top of one is not severed, it is fit.

chunks.en: Rabbi Tarfon says,
chunks.st: Rabbi Tarfon says:

chunks.en: even if all three are cut at the top.
chunks.st: Even if the tops of all three are severed, it is fit.

chunks.en: Rabbi Akiva says,
chunks.st: Rabbi Akiva says with regard to the number of each of the species:

chunks.en: just as there is one lulav and one esrog,
chunks.st: Just as there is one lulav and one etrog,

chunks.en: so there is one hadas and one aravah.
chunks.st: so too there is one myrtle branch and one willow branch.

summary: An esrog that is stolen, dried out, from avodah zarah, orlah or tamei terumah is not kosher. Some kinds of esrog should not be used at first, but if used they are kosher.

chunks.en: An esrog that is stolen or dried out
chunks.st: An etrog that was stolen or is completely dry

chunks.he: פָּסוּל. שֶׁל אֲשֵׁרָה וְשֶׁל עִיר הַנִּדַּחַת,
chunks.en: is not kosher. One from an asheirah tree or from a city that served idols
chunks.st: is unfit. One from a tree worshipped as idolatry [asheira] or from a city whose residents were incited to idolatry

chunks.en: is not kosher. One that is orlah
chunks.explain: Fruit from a tree's first three years, which is forbidden.
chunks.st: is unfit. An etrog that is fruit that grew on a tree during the three years after it was planted [orla]

chunks.en: is not kosher. One of terumah that is tamei
chunks.st: is unfit, because it is prohibited to eat and derive benefit from it. An etrog of impure teruma

words.note: A gift of food for the Kohanim.

chunks.en: is not kosher. One of terumah that is tahor:
chunks.st: is unfit. With regard to an etrog of pure teruma,

chunks.en: he should not take it,
chunks.st: one may not take it ab initio,

chunks.en: but if he took it,
chunks.st: and if one took it,

chunks.en: it is kosher. One of demai:
chunks.explain: Demai is food bought from someone who may not have taken off ma'aser.
chunks.st: it is fit, and he fulfilled his obligation after the fact. With regard to an etrog of demai,
chunks.stMore: which is produce acquired from an am ha’aretz, who does not reliably tithe his produce,

chunks.en: Beis Shammai say it is not kosher,
chunks.st: Beit Shammai deem it unfit,

chunks.en: and Beis Hillel say it is kosher.
chunks.st: and Beit Hillel deem it fit.

chunks.en: One of ma'aser sheni in Yerushalayim:
chunks.explain: Ma'aser sheni is a tenth of the crops, eaten in Yerushalayim.
chunks.st: With regard to an etrog of second tithe in Jerusalem,

chunks.en: he should not take it,
chunks.st: one may not take it ab initio;

chunks.en: but if he took it, it is kosher.
chunks.st: and if he took it, it is fit.

summary: An esrog with spots on most of it, or that lost its tip, or is peeled, split or has a hole with a piece missing, is not kosher. A black esrog is not kosher, and Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda argue about a green one.

chunks.en: If spots grew over most of it,
chunks.st: If boil-like blemishes arose on the majority of the etrog;

chunks.en: if its pitam was taken off,
chunks.explain: The pitam is the little tip at the top of the esrog.
chunks.st: if its pestle-like protuberance on the upper, blossom end was removed;

chunks.en: if it was peeled, if it was split,
chunks.st: if the etrog was peeled, split,

chunks.en: or it has a hole and is missing any bit,
chunks.st: or pierced and is missing any amount,

chunks.en: it is not kosher. If spots grew over a small part of it,
chunks.st: it is unfit. However, if boil-like blemishes arose only on its minority;

chunks.en: if its stem was taken off,
chunks.st: if its stem, which connects it to the tree, was removed;

chunks.en: or it has a hole but nothing is missing,
chunks.st: or it was pierced but is not missing any amount,

chunks.en: it is kosher. A black esrog
chunks.st: it is fit. A Cushite etrog,
chunks.stMore: which is black like a Cushite,

chunks.en: is not kosher. And one as green as a leek:
chunks.st: is unfit. And with regard to an etrog that is leek green,

chunks.en: Rabbi Meir says it is kosher,
chunks.st: Rabbi Meir deems it fit

chunks.en: and Rabbi Yehuda says it is not kosher.
chunks.st: and Rabbi Yehuda deems it unfit.

summary: How small or how big may an esrog be? Rabbi Meir, Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Yosei give different sizes.

chunks.en: The smallest size of an esrog:
chunks.st: What is the minimum measure of a small etrog?

chunks.en: Rabbi Meir says,
chunks.st: Rabbi Meir says:

chunks.en: like a walnut. Rabbi Yehuda says,
chunks.st: It may be no smaller than a walnut-bulk. Rabbi Yehuda says:

chunks.en: like an egg. And the biggest size:
chunks.st: It may be no smaller than an egg-bulk. And in a large

chunks.en: small enough to hold two in one hand,
chunks.st: etrog, the maximum measure is so that one could hold two in his one hand;

chunks.en: says Rabbi Yehuda.
chunks.st: this is the statement of Rabbi Yehuda.

chunks.en: Rabbi Yosei says,
chunks.st: Rabbi Yosei says:

chunks.en: even if he can hold only one with both hands.
chunks.st: It is fit even if it is so large that he can hold only one in his two hands.

summary: Rabbi Yehuda says the lulav must be tied with something from its own kind. Rabbi Meir says any string is fine, and tells about the people of Yerushalayim who used gold bands.

chunks.he: אֵין אוֹגְדִין אֶת הַלּוּלָב אֶלָּא בְמִינוֹ,
chunks.en: We may tie the lulav only with its own kind,
chunks.explain: With a part of a palm tree or of the other minim.
chunks.st: One may bind the lulav only with its own species;
chunks.stMore: i.e., one of the four species taken with the lulav.

chunks.en: says Rabbi Yehuda.
chunks.st: This is the statement of Rabbi Yehuda.

chunks.en: Rabbi Meir says,
chunks.st: Rabbi Meir says:

chunks.en: even with a string.
chunks.st: One may do so even with a string or with a cord.

chunks.en: Rabbi Meir said,
chunks.st: Rabbi Meir said:

chunks.en: there was a story with the people of Yerushalayim,
chunks.st: There was an incident involving the men of Jerusalem

chunks.en: who used to tie their lulavim
chunks.st: who would bind their lulavim

chunks.en: with bands of gold.
chunks.st: with gold rings.

chunks.en: They said to him,
chunks.st: The Sages said to him:

chunks.en: they tied it with its own kind underneath.
chunks.explain: The gold was only to make it look nice.
chunks.st: They would bind it with its own species beneath the rings, which serve a merely decorative purpose and not a halakhic one.

summary: This mishnah teaches where in Hallel we shake the lulav. If someone did not take the lulav on the way or in the morning, he may take it later, because the whole day is good for the lulav.

chunks.en: And where did they shake the lulav?
chunks.st: And where in the recitation of hallel would they wave the lulav?

chunks.en: At "Hodu laShem," at the beginning and the end,
chunks.st: They would do so at the verse: “Thank the Lord, for He is good” (Psalms 118:1, 29) that appears at both the beginning and the end of the psalm,

chunks.en: and at "Ana Hashem hoshi'ah na,"
chunks.st: and at the verse: “Lord, please save us” (Psalms 118:25);

chunks.en: says Beis Hillel.
chunks.st: this is the statement of Beit Hillel.

chunks.en: And Beis Shammai say,
chunks.st: And Beit Shammai say:

chunks.en: also at "Ana Hashem hatzlichah na."
chunks.explain: This means "Please, Hashem, give us success."
chunks.st: They would wave the lulav even at the verse: “Lord, please grant us success” (Psalms 118:25).

chunks.en: Rabbi Akiva said,
chunks.st: Rabbi Akiva said:

chunks.he: צוֹפֶה הָיִיתִי בְרַבָּן גַּמְלִיאֵל וּבְרַבִּי יְהוֹשֻׁעַ,
chunks.en: I watched Rabban Gamliel and Rabbi Yehoshua:
chunks.st: I was observing Rabban Gamliel and Rabbi Yehoshua

chunks.he: שֶׁכָּל הָעָם הָיוּ מְנַעְנְעִים אֶת לוּלְבֵיהֶן,
chunks.en: all the people were shaking their lulavim,
chunks.st: and saw that all the people were waving their lulavim,

chunks.en: but they shook only
chunks.st: and the two of them waved their lulav only at:

chunks.en: at "Ana Hashem hoshi'ah na."
chunks.st: “Lord, please save us,”
chunks.stMore: indicating that this is the halakha.

chunks.en: Someone who was traveling and did not
chunks.st: With regard to one who was coming along the way and did not

chunks.en: have a lulav to take,
chunks.st: have a lulav in his hand to take
chunks.stMore: and fulfill the mitzva while traveling,

chunks.en: when he comes into his house, he should take it at his table.
chunks.st: when he enters his house to eat,he should take the lulav at his table.
chunks.stMore: He interrupts his meal to fulfill the mitzva of lulav.

chunks.en: If he did not take it in the morning,
chunks.st: If he did not take the lulav in the morning,

chunks.en: he should take it in the afternoon,
chunks.st: he should take it in the afternoon,

chunks.en: because the whole day is good for the lulav.
chunks.st: as the entire day is suited for fulfilling the mitzva of lulav.

summary: If someone cannot say Hallel by himself, and a servant, woman or child says it for him, he must repeat every word. If a grown man says it for him, he just answers "Halleluyah."

chunks.en: Someone for whom a servant or a woman
chunks.st: With regard to one for whom a Canaanite slave, a woman,

chunks.en: or a child was saying Hallel,
chunks.st: or a minor was reciting hallel,

chunks.en: must repeat after them what they say.
chunks.st: he repeats after them what they are saying word for word.

chunks.en: And a curse should come on him!
chunks.explain: For not learning to say it himself.
chunks.st: The mishna notes: And may a curse come to him
chunks.stMore: for being so ignorant that he needs them to recite it for him.

chunks.en: If a grown man was saying it for him,
chunks.st: If an adult male was reciting hallel on his
chunks.stMore: behalf, he need not repeat each word, as the adult male can fulfill the obligation to recite hallel on his behalf. Rather,

chunks.en: he answers after him "Halleluyah."
chunks.st: he simply answers: Halleluya, to each phrase that is recited.

summary: In saying Hallel and its bracha, everyone follows the custom of his place. During shemittah, someone buying a lulav from a person who may not keep shemittah gets the esrog as a gift.

chunks.en: In a place where they are used to repeating verses,
chunks.st: In a place where they were accustomed to repeat certain verses,

chunks.en: he should repeat them. To say them once,
chunks.st: he, too, should repeat them. If the custom is to recite them plainly,

chunks.en: he should say them once. To make a bracha after it,
chunks.st: without repetition, he should recite them plainly. In a place where the custom is to recite a blessing after hallel,

chunks.en: he should make a bracha after it.
chunks.st: he should recite a blessing.

chunks.en: Everything follows the custom of the place.
chunks.st: Everything is in accordance with the local custom in these matters.

chunks.en: Someone who buys a lulav from his friend in the shemittah year
chunks.explain: Shemittah is the seventh year, when fruit may not be bought and sold like usual.
chunks.st: In the case of one who purchases a lulav from another who is an am ha’aretz during the Sabbatical Year,

chunks.en: should get the esrog as a gift,
chunks.st: the seller gives him an etrog along with it as a gift,

chunks.en: because he may not buy it in shemittah.
chunks.st: as he is not permitted to purchase the etrog during the Sabbatical Year because it is prohibited to engage in commerce with Sabbatical-Year produce.

summary: In the time of the Beis HaMikdash, the lulav was taken all seven days only in the Beis HaMikdash. After it was destroyed, Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai made a rule to take it everywhere for seven days, to remember the Beis HaMikdash.

chunks.he: בָּרִאשׁוֹנָה הָיָה לוּלָב נִטָּל בַּמִּקְדָּשׁ שִׁבְעָה,
chunks.en: At first, the lulav was taken in the Beis HaMikdash for seven days,
chunks.st: Originally, during the Temple era, the lulav was taken in the Temple for seven days,

chunks.en: and everywhere else for one day.
chunks.st: and in the rest of the country outside the Temple it was taken for one day.

chunks.en: When the Beis HaMikdash was destroyed,
chunks.st: Once the Temple was destroyed,

chunks.en: Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai made a rule
chunks.st: Rabban Yoḥanan ben Zakkai instituted an ordinance

chunks.en: that the lulav should be taken everywhere for seven days,
chunks.st: that the lulav should be taken even in the rest of the country for seven days,

chunks.en: to remember the Beis HaMikdash.
chunks.st: in commemoration of the Temple.

chunks.en: And that the whole day of waving the omer should be forbidden.
chunks.explain: On that day we may not eat from the new grain.
chunks.st: And for similar reasons, he instituted an ordinance that for the entire day of waving the omer offering, it should be prohibited to eat the grain of the new crop.
chunks.stMore: It is prohibited to eat the grain of the new crop until the omer offering is brought and waved in the Temple on the sixteenth of Nisan. The offering was sacrificed in the morning; however, after taking potential delays into consideration, the new crop remained prohibited until it was clear that the offering had been sacrificed. Practically speaking, it was prohibited to eat the new grain until the sixteenth of Nisan was over; it was permitted only on the seventeenth. Once the Temple was destroyed and there was no longer an omer offering sacrificed, it was permitted to eat the new crop on the sixteenth. However, Rabban Yoḥanan instituted an ordinance that eating the new grain would remain prohibited until the seventeenth to commemorate the Temple.

words.note: The day the omer offering was waved in the Beis HaMikdash.

summary: When the first day of Sukkos is on Shabbos, people bring their lulavim to shul before Shabbos. On the first day a person must use his own lulav, but on the other days he may use his friend's.

chunks.en: The first day of
chunks.st: If the first day of

chunks.en: the chag, if it falls on Shabbos,
chunks.st: the festival of Sukkot occurs on Shabbat,

chunks.en: all the people bring
chunks.st: all of the people bring their

chunks.en: their lulavim to the shul.
chunks.explain: They bring them before Shabbos, since we may not carry outside on Shabbos.
chunks.st: lulavim to the synagogue
chunks.stMore: on Shabbat eve, as it is prohibited to carry in a public domain on Shabbat.

chunks.en: The next day, they come early,
chunks.st: The next day, on Shabbat, everyone rises early and comes to the synagogue.

chunks.he: כָּל אֶחָד וְאֶחָד מַכִּיר אֶת שֶׁלּוֹ,
chunks.en: and each one finds his own lulav
chunks.st: Each and every one recognizes his lulav

chunks.en: and takes it. Because the Sages said,
chunks.st: and takes it. This emphasis that each and every one recognizes his own lulav and takes it is because the Sages said:

chunks.en: a person does not do his mitzvah
chunks.st: A person does not fulfill his obligation to take the lulav

chunks.en: on the first day of the chag
chunks.st: on the first day of the Festival

chunks.en: with his friend's lulav.
chunks.st: with the lulav of another,

chunks.en: But on the other days of the chag,
chunks.st: and on the rest of the days of the Festival

chunks.en: a person does his mitzvah
chunks.st: a person fulfills his obligation

chunks.en: with his friend's lulav.
chunks.st: even with the lulav of another.

summary: Rabbi Yosei says that if someone forgot it was Shabbos and carried his lulav outside, he does not need to bring a korban, because he was busy with a mitzvah.

chunks.en: Rabbi Yosei says,
chunks.st: Rabbi Yosei says:

chunks.en: the first day of
chunks.st: If the first day of

chunks.en: the chag, if it falls on Shabbos,
chunks.st: the Festival occurs on Shabbat,

chunks.he: וְשָׁכַח וְהוֹצִיא אֶת הַלּוּלָב לִרְשׁוּת הָרַבִּים,
chunks.en: and he forgot and carried the lulav out to a public place,
chunks.st: and he forgot and carried the lulav out into the public domain,

chunks.en: he does not have to bring a korban, because he carried it with permission.
chunks.explain: He was busy with the mitzvah of lulav.
chunks.st: he is exempt from liability to bring a sin-offering for this unwitting transgression because he carried it out with permission,
chunks.stMore: i.e., he was preoccupied with the performance of the mitzva and carried it out.

summary: On Shabbos and Yom Tov we may put the lulav back in water to keep it fresh. A child who knows how to shake the lulav must take one.

chunks.en: A woman may take the lulav from her son or from
chunks.st: A woman may receive a lulav from her son or from

chunks.en: her husband, and put it back in the water on Shabbos.
chunks.st: her husband and return it on Shabbat to the water in which it had been placed.

chunks.en: Rabbi Yehuda says,
chunks.st: Rabbi Yehuda says:

chunks.en: on Shabbos we put it back,
chunks.st: On Shabbat one may return the lulav to the water;

chunks.en: on Yom Tov we may add water,
chunks.st: and on the Festival one may even add fresh water to the vessel so the lulav will not wilt;

chunks.en: and on Chol HaMoed we may change the water.
chunks.st: and during the intermediate days of the Festival, one may even change the water.

chunks.en: A child who knows how to shake the lulav
chunks.st: A minor who knows how to wave the lulav

chunks.en: must take the lulav.
chunks.explain: So that he learns to do mitzvos.
chunks.st: is obligated in the mitzva of lulav due to the requirement to train him in the performance of mitzvot.
